5.text: On the Pacific shore some native blacksmiths, Chukchee and Eskimo,

6.text: hammer traps of their own out of the bar-iron bought from whalers. They

7.text: have usually but one spring; since traps with two springs work too strongly,

8.text: and often cut off the paw, instead of holding it. Both kinds of spring-traps,

9.text: especially the larger ones of steel, are used also for other animals, — hares,

10.text: wolverines, wolves, and even swans and geese. When set for the wolf, the

11.text: steel trap is fastened with a strong chain to a wooden block weighing from

12.text: twenty to twenty-five pounds, so that the wolf may be able to drag it along

13.text: on the snow. If the block should be too heavy, the wolf would snap the

14.text: chain and carry away the trap. Sometimes the wolf that carried away the

15.text: trap is able to live for several months on the tundra, preying on hares, moulting

16.text: ducks, etc. Once in the winter I was shown, on the fresh trail of several

17.text: wolves, the footsteps of one that evidently had only three paws; the fourth

18.text: paw probably having withered, and dropped down with the trap. Another

19.text: time a trap carried away by a wolf in the fall was found in the spring far

20.text: away in the tundra, with the withered paw of a wolf in it.

21.text: Dead-falls are used only by a few Chukchee, in imitation of the Russians,

22.text: who have large rows of them everywhere in the forest and on the tundra.

27.text: A common fox dead-fall (Fig. 49) consists of a double fence made of

28.text: thin poles ten feet long and two feet high, with a space between about two

29.text: feet and a half broad. The flooring is laid loosely; and the roof is formed

30.text: of two or three strong beams split at the front end, and having a cross-pole

31.text: jammed into the cleft. The rear end simply rests on the ground or on a

32.text: special, very low support. Sometimes a large stone is put on the roof to
